per_question.question: What medical loss ratio (MLR) must Medicaid managed care organizations meet under federal law, and how does NC implement this requirement?
per_question.agent_answer:
Under federal law, Medicaid managed care organizations are **not automatically subject to a universal minimum MLR**. Instead, the federal rule requires states to ensure that each MCO, PIHP, and PAHP **calculates and reports** an MLR, and **if** a state chooses to impose a minimum MLR, that minimum must be **at least 85%**. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

## Federal rule

### 1) What is required in all states
For contracts starting on or after July 1, 2017, the state must ensure through its managed care contracts that each MCO, PIHP, and PAHP **calculates and reports** an MLR in accordance with the federal methodology. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8(a)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

### 2) When an actual minimum applies
Federal law says that **if a state elects to mandate a minimum MLR**, that minimum must be **equal to or higher than 85 percent**. So the federal floor for any state-imposed minimum is 85%; the regulation does **not** say every Medicaid MCO nationwide must meet 85% absent state adoption of a minimum. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8(c)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

### 3) Oversight and remittances
If a state requires a minimum MLR, it must annually submit to CMS a summary of each plan’s MLR reporting, including the numerator, denominator, MLR percentage, member months, and any remittances owed. If the state requires remittances for failure to meet the minimum, the state must reimburse CMS for the federal share and submit a separate methodology report. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.74](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

## North Carolina implementation

North Carolina’s implementation evidence I was able to verify here is in **SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care**, which states that if an MCO, PIHP, or PAHP owes a remittance for failing to meet the state-required minimum MLR, North Carolina will reimburse CMS for the federal share and submit the required separate report describing the state/federal share methodology. [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care, § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment)

That SPA text supports the conclusion that North Carolina implements the federal framework by recognizing:
- a **state-required minimum MLR** structure,
- possible **remittances** if the minimum is not met, and
- the associated **CMS reporting and federal-share repayment** obligations. [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care, § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment); [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.74](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)

## Bottom line

- **Federal law:** MCOs must **calculate and report** MLR; a **minimum MLR is optional for the state**, but if imposed it must be **at least 85%**. [42 CFR Part 438, § 438.8](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-42/part-438)
- **North Carolina:** The NC SPA text I verified shows North Carolina has adopted the **reporting/remittance framework** tied to a state-required minimum MLR, including repayment of the federal share of remittances and separate reporting to CMS. [SPA 22-0013 Proposed Amendments CHIP-Managed Care, § 3.3](https://medicaid.ncdhhs.gov/22-0013-proposed-amendment-chip-managed-care/download?attachment)

I could not verify from the retrieved NC text alone any more detailed state contract wording beyond that excerpt.

scores.explanation: The agent's answer is factually accurate on the key points: states must require MCOs to calculate and report MLR, the minimum MLR floor is 85% if a state elects to mandate one, and remittance requirements apply. These align precisely with 42 CFR 438.8(a) and (c). The agent correctly distinguishes between the mandatory reporting requirement and the optional minimum MLR standard. The NC implementation section is thin but honest about limitations, referencing a SPA document. The answer lacks detail on the MLR calculation methodology (numerator/denominator components, credibility adjustments, aggregation rules, reporting requirements) that the reference evidence covers extensively. Citation quality is adequate with specific regulatory section references (438.8(a), 438.8(c), 438.74) but misses many subsections. No hallucinations are present - the agent is careful to note what it could and couldn't verify. The overall answer would be acceptable to a Medicaid policy expert as a summary but incomplete for detailed policy work.
